claims.text: The investigated alloy is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The starting alloy has an fcc matrix.
The as-fabricated alloy is fully single-phase fcc.
The as-fabricated alloy has high strength and fatigue resistance.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by the formation and integrity of a continuous, thin Al/Ti-rich oxide scale.
The proposed Al/Ti-rich protective scale forms only under oxidizing conditions.
A continuous Al/Ti-rich scale retards oxygen ingress into the alloy.
The protective oxide scale preserves the integrity of the fcc matrix.
Selective oxidation of Al and Ti produces the proposed protective oxide layer.
Under reducing conditions, the protective oxide layer is absent or unstable.
Absence or instability of the protective layer under reducing conditions permits more rapid internal oxygen penetration and internal oxidation.
Reducing exposure promotes microstructural or phase destabilization.
Oxidizing exposure at about 750 °C will produce a thin, continuous Al/Ti-rich oxide scale.
Oxidizing exposure will cause less internal oxidation and less mechanical-property loss than reducing exposure.
Reducing exposure will produce heterogeneous or incomplete oxide formation.
Reducing exposure will accelerate degradation of strength and fatigue resistance relative to the as-fabricated baseline.
Exposure near 750 °C is relevant to microstructural evolution in this Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti alloy system.
The proposed comparison is scoped to approximately 750 °C and exposure durations of 10–50 hours.
The hypothesis may not apply at lower temperatures or under transient thermal conditions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the Al/Ti-rich scale forms only under oxidizing conditions and describes its absence under reducing conditions, while the predicted outcome allows heterogeneous or incomplete oxide formation under reducing conditions.

The reducing condition is exemplified as H2-diluted inert gas, yet it is predicted to permit more rapid oxygen penetration and increased internal oxidation without specifying a residual oxygen or water activity capable of supplying that oxygen.
